title: Kaam: desire kept, not killed
hookLine: kaam: desire put in its place by discipline and love
carry: kaam: not killed, not crowned, kept

lines: MIDNIGHT, AND THE PHONE LIGHTS UP.
cards: Midnight, and the phone lights up. A dessert, a stranger's photo, an ad that seems to know exactly what to show. Desire is no stranger to human life.
It gets people out of bed, into kitchens, into marriages, into music and art. The question the Gurus press isn't whether it's there. It's where it sits: in the passenger seat, or behind the wheel.
Today's thief is kaam: desire, and above all the pull of lust. The Sikh answer isn't to kill it. It's to put it in its place.

teach.b: First, the warning. Kaam opens the Gurus' list of thieves. In the same run of saloks that cried out to anger a few days ago, Guru Arjan turns to desire.
In paraphrase: O desire, you lead people to hell and set them wandering from life to life; you steal the mind, you reach across the worlds, you tear apart meditation, discipline and good conduct.
Strong language, and it's meant to be. Unruled, desire takes the wheel. Second, the householder.
And yet the Sikh answer is not celibacy, and not a monastery.
The Sikh path is a householder's path, and the Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, is a sacred rite: the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib while the Lavan, hymns of Guru Ram Das, are sung.
Desire inside a faithful, committed love isn't a thief breaking in. It's family, living at home. Third, the discipline.

The Sikh code of conduct asks for faithfulness in marriage, and in Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan describes a person of God as one whose eyes don't look on another's wife with desire. Restraint here isn't hatred of the body.
It's keeping a promise, with the eyes as well as the hands.
Fourth, love as the rein. Discipline alone is a fence, and fences get climbed. The Gurus pair it with love for the One, so the heart's deepest wanting has somewhere true to go.
The pull doesn't vanish; it gets pointed.
Desire in its place: not killed, not crowned. Kept.

how: Sikhs count kaam among the five thieves and meet it not with celibacy but with married, faithful householder life, the discipline of the Sikh code of conduct and the remembrance of the Name.

games.q: what does “desire in its place” mean?
o: desire kept in bounds by discipline and love
desire crushed out completely by willpower
desire followed freely wherever it leads

games.q: desire in its place: tap the pairs.
p: the Sikh wedding, around the Granth

s: Sikhism asks for celibacy to beat kaam
the Sikh path is a householder's path; the Sikh wedding is a sacred rite.
Guru Arjan warns that unruled desire tears apart meditation and discipline
in a salok he says it steals the mind and tears apart meditation, discipline and good conduct.
in Sikh teaching, restraint means hating the body
restraint is keeping a promise; love gives desire somewhere true to go.

games.q: a pull shows up that would mean breaking a promise you made. what does today's teaching point toward?
o: pause a breath, and keep the promise.
hate yourself for feeling it at all.
games.why: the Gurus don't ask anyone to hate the body. they ask for restraint and faithful love: desire in its place.

practice: Bring to mind one pull that tends to grab the wheel, a late-night scroll, a second helping, a look that lingers, a purchase at midnight, and name it gently, without shame: there you are.
Picture the moment it's likely to show up, and see yourself pausing for one full breath and choosing, this once, not to follow it. If you pray, ask for steadiness in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Desire in its place. Kaam, desire and lust, ruled by discipline and pointed by love: in the Sikh answer, not killed and not crowned. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: desire, especially lust; in the Granth often ਕਾਮੁ.

carryVoice: Your line: kaam, not killed, not crowned, kept. A pull can wait a breath at the door. Until tomorrow.
